title: From a port list to a compose file: how MediaBox started

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Antoine kept forgetting what was running on port eight thousand ninety-six. So he started writing a list. That list grew into a GitHub project called MediaBoxDockerCompose.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: A to-do list of apps that turns into a repo. What's actually in it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: One docker compose file, shared storage paths on disk, and lessons from breaking things at home. He uses it when he wants one host, many containers, shared volumes. So Jellyfin next to Deluge next to FreshRSS, without a new container per hobby.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: He says it gives library playback without the Plex account drama. And Plex, Sonarr and Radarr are still bookmarks, not in the compose file today.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Things he actually kept. Netdata, for the is-the-disk-full-again glance. Guacamole, for remote desktop in a browser tab. BookStack for homelab docs. Gitea for git experiments before pushing to GitHub. And he picked ports in families starting with eight hundred, which made life easier behind Caddy.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And what if compose isn't the right shape?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Then he uses the Proxmox VE Helper-Scripts. They're community one-liners you paste into the Proxmox shell, and you get a container plus a post-install menu for updates. He's run compose on one VM and separate containers from those scripts on the same rack, depending on whether he wanted shared volumes or hard isolation.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: No. His line is to pick compose or Proxmox scripts for the shape of the problem, not because a blog post said one is cooler.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And the famous list? How long did it get?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The original sheet had eighty-six Docker names, plus dozens never wired up. He doesn't paste it, because it ages badly and reads like a status dashboard.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Plan ports in families, and remember that running something once isn't the same as operating it. The README in the repo is the real manual, and the full post has the service tables.
